claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability is primarily governed by entropy-driven stabilization of the solid-solution phase.
A maximally equiatomic five-element composition has greater configurational entropy than a composition in which one element is reduced to 5 at%.
Increasing configurational entropy by making the composition maximally equiatomic will enhance stability relative to less-equiatomic or binary compositions.
The initial nanoparticles are single-phase, multi-element, near-equiatomic solid solutions, exemplified by five-element alloys containing approximately 20 at% of each element.
Reducing one component from approximately 20 at% to 5 at% while increasing the other components proportionally provides a controlled change in equiatomicity.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the solid-solution phase.
High configurational entropy lowers the free-energy barrier for phase segregation.
High configurational entropy lowers the free-energy barrier for diffusion.
The proposed entropy effect reduces elemental clustering, phase separation, and surface enrichment during thermal exposure.
After identical high-temperature exposure, maximally equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit less phase segregation than less-equiatomic variants.
After identical high-temperature exposure, maximally equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit lower elemental diffusion rates than less-equiatomic variants.
After identical high-temperature exposure, maximally equiatomic nanoparticles will retain a more uniform elemental distribution than less-equiatomic variants.
STEM-EDS, XRD, and surface analysis can detect the predicted differences in elemental distribution, phase purity, and surface enrichment.
The hypothesis applies to single-phase solid-solution nanoparticles containing at least four elements over the stated catalytic and thermoelectric temperature ranges.
Strong elemental immiscibility or large atomic-size mismatch may prevent the proposed entropy-based stabilization.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says configurational entropy suppresses segregation and diffusion, whereas the mechanism says it lowers the barriers for segregation and diffusion. Lower barriers would ordinarily facilitate those processes rather than suppress them.

The intervention proposes changing an element from about 20 at% to 5 at% and adjusting the other fractions while also saying that overall composition is held constant. The elemental fractions cannot both change and remain compositionally constant; only constituent identity, particle size, and processing could be held constant.

A binary baseline is not compositionally matched to the proposed same-five-element equiatomicity intervention and also falls outside the stated boundary of at least four elements, so it does not isolate equiatomicity from element-count and chemical-identity effects.
